summary: This informational memo updates RFC 1816 and describes registration policies for the .GOV top-level domain, meant to give US federal agencies recognizable names. It aims to avoid name duplication and limit registrations to appropriate agencies.

eli5.summary: Rules for who can have a web address ending in .gov, kept for the national government.

questions: one agency one name dns policy
subtitle: The Federal Networking Council's rules for who may register a name directly under .GOV: one agency, one name.

tldr.problem: Agencies of the US federal government had registered many overlapping names under .GOV, which caused duplication and made the space confusing for the public and heavy for the registration authority.
tldr.mechanism: The policy limits .GOV to federal-level entities listed in FIPS 95-1 or the US Government Manual, allows only one registration per agency, and tells subsidiary components to register beneath their parent.
tldr.outcome: Existing duplicate names get until August 1998 to be resolved. The memo is Informational and replaces RFC 1816.

today: RFC 2146 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1816. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo does not claim to be an Internet standard.

sections.title: What the Policy Covers
sections.content:
This memo updates and clarifies RFC 1816. It describes the registration policy for the top-level domain .GOV, which exists to give naming conventions that identify US Federal government agencies and make their electronic resources easier to reach. The domain is delegated from the root authority to the US Federal Networking Council (FNC).

The memo restricts registrations to match the approved structure of the US government and the advice of its Chief Information Officers (CIOs). As a side effect it reduces the number of .GOV and FED.US registrations and the workload of the registration authority. Earlier versions did not address the FED.US domain; the memo says references to .GOV apply to FED.US as well and anticipates .GOV migrating into FED.US.

.GOV is for the federal level only. State and local governments are to register under the .US domain.
sections.eli5: The .gov part of a web address is reserved for the national government. Cities and states are told to use a different ending.

sections.title: Who May Register
sections.content:
The short form of the policy is one agency, one name. The agency may pick its own name, but an easily recognized acronym is suggested. Two documents decide eligibility: FIPS 95-1 ("Codes for the Identification of Federal and Federally Assisted Organizations") and the US Government Manual.

  • Top-level entities, such as departments, independent establishments, boards, commissions and committees, and independent agencies like the National Science Foundation, can register directly under .GOV.
  • Cross-agency collaborative organizations, such as the Federal Networking Council, can register on presenting their chartering document. They are the only organizations not listed in FIPS 95-1 or the Manual that may do so.
  • Subsidiary, non-autonomous components are not eligible. They register as third-level domains under their parent, or may apply to FED.US.
  • Federally Aided Organizations in FIPS 95-1 should use .ORG or another suitable top-level domain.
  • Organizations subsidiary to the Department of Defense register under .MIL.
  • Federal courts are a special class. SUPREME-COURT is reserved for the Supreme Court, and all other courts register in .USCOURTS.GOV.

Other entities may be registered at the request of a cognizant CIO. Exceptions for changes not yet reflected in the listed documents need documentation and are otherwise referred to the FNC.
sections.eli5: Big official offices get their own name. Smaller parts of an office share their parent's name, and some groups, like the military and the courts, have their own special places to sign up.

sections.title: Naming and Registration Rules
sections.content:
A domain name should be derived from the organization's official name, for example USDA.Gov or AGRICULTURE.GOV. The registration is listed under the official name from FIPS 95-1 or the Manual, or under the name in the chartering document.

Only one registration and delegation is made to identify an agency, and registrations are first-come first-served. Which part of the agency manages the space beneath its domain is the agency's own business.

Agencies that already had several registrations under .GOV may keep them until August 1998, but sub-delegations are allowed only under the one chosen permanent name. As of August 1996 the auxiliary domains become un-delegated and revert to the .GOV owner. As of 2 August 1997 every auxiliary registration must be mirrored in the permanent domain, and at the three year point all auxiliary registrations are deleted (August 1998).

Entities already in .GOV but not listed in FIPS 95-1 or the Manual, such as DOE labs and state entities, may keep their registration under the single-registration rule, but no further non-listed registrations are made. State and local entities are strongly encouraged, but not required, to move to .US.
sections.eli5: Each agency gets one name. Anyone who had extra names was given a few years to give them back, and the old ones that still work are allowed to stay.

sections.title: Clarifications and FAQ
sections.content:
The memo adds a clarification section and a long list of questions and answers. Registrations from before August 1995 are grandfathered, except for duplicates of the same organization at the same level: two registrations for the Department of Transportation would be duplicates, but one each for the Department and the FAA would not, because the FAA is an autonomous component.

Examples given for names that had to resolve duplicates include STATE.GOV and LABOR.GOV. Examples of grandfathered names are CDC.GOV, NIH.GOV and LBL.GOV. Names inside an agency's own delegation, such as cdc.dhhs.gov, are the business of that agency.

The FAQ also covers advertising through domain names, which it says is not encouraged. It advises that an agency worried about lookalike names in other top-level domains can register its name in all available domains and hold them unused, and that using domains other than .GOV or FED.US is a policy matter for the Office of Management and Budget. On resolution cost, it explains that caching and co-located servers keep extra DNS queries small, and that CNAME records can ease moving between name spaces.
sections.eli5: The question-and-answer part is like a school handbook: it says what happens to old names, what counts as the same office, and who to ask when you are unsure.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo notes that the integrity of DNS data, as made available through network protocols, is not reliable on the Internet without extra cryptographic controls or secure lines. Agencies with secure internal lines may trust internal naming information, but Internet users cannot.

DNS may be enhanced with digital signatures on the information it serves. When that software becomes available, .GOV second-level domain administrators are encouraged to use it to give a secure binding for the information tied to their names.
sections.eli5: Anyone could try to fake a name-to-address answer. The memo says that once signed answers are available, government sites should use them so people know the answer is real.
